sections.title: Live case: Sarah Wilkinson, reported particulars only
sections.intro: Selected for closer research on 10 November 2026. While the case is active we report only the offences charged, the court, adjournments and bail, and explain the general law. The next section examines section 58 and independent research. See What we can say, and what we can’t, for why.

entries.title: Seven counts; trial listed
entries.kind: Dated court reporting · limited to the reportable particulars

paragraphs.text: Court reporting from 24 June 2026 records seven counts before Birmingham Crown Court: two of encouragement of terrorism, two of expressing an opinion or belief supportive of a proscribed organisation, two of disseminating a terrorist publication, and one of failing to comply with a notice under section 49 of the Regulation of Investigatory Powers Act 2000. Bail was continued and a trial is listed for 4 January 2027. Because the counts require a preparatory hearing, we keep to the particulars a report of one may contain until the court confirms which restrictions apply. She is presumed innocent.

entries.title: RIPA: what the separate compliance offence requires
entries.kind: Legislation · general explanation, not a finding about this defendant

paragraphs.text: Part III of the Regulation of Investigatory Powers Act 2000 provides for notices requiring disclosure of protected information. Section 49 requires appropriate permission and reasonable grounds, including necessity, proportionality and the impracticability of obtaining intelligible information without a notice. The notice must identify the required disclosure and allow a reasonable compliance period. These are statutory requirements to examine against the actual notice.

Section 53 concerns knowingly failing to make the disclosure required by a section 49 notice. It also addresses possession of a key, the criminal standard for the contrary case once sufficient evidence of non-possession is raised, and a defence concerning disclosure as soon as reasonably practicable. These provisions are more specific than a general allegation of not cooperating with police.

On indictment the usual maximum is two years; it is five years where the notice’s specified grounds include national security, or in the separately defined child-indecency category. A terrorism-related investigation alone does not establish which maximum applies. The notice itself shows which maximum applies in a given case.

sections.title: Research, reasonable excuse and section 58
sections.intro: The reported counts in the Wilkinson case are encouragement, support, dissemination and a separate RIPA compliance offence, not section 58. The general law of section 58 still matters for anyone researching the same subject matter: collecting or accessing certain material is a different question from publishing it or expressing a view. This section explains that distinction. It is general legal explanation, not a finding about this defendant.

entries.title: Section 58: what the law actually says
entries.kind: Legislation · general explanation, not a finding about this defendant

paragraphs.text: A person does not have to be a university researcher to potentially have a reasonable excuse under section 58 of the Terrorism Act 2000. There is a major legal distinction between researching terrorist material and publishing or distributing it.
The cases in which a person has a reasonable excuse for the purposes of subsection (3) include (but are not limited to) those in which—

That phrase means Parliament expressly recognised certain reasonable excuses without making them an exhaustive list. Under section 58, collecting or recording information of a kind likely to be useful to a person committing or preparing an act of terrorism, possessing a document or record containing it, or viewing or otherwise accessing such a document by means of the internet, can constitute an offence. Section 58(3) provides a reasonable-excuse defence. Section 58(3A) expressly identifies circumstances including: not knowing, and having no reason to believe, that the document or record contained, or was likely to contain, information of that kind; carrying out work as a journalist; and conducting academic research.

An independent researcher investigating the history of Hamas, the events of 7 October 2023 or competing narratives about Operation Al-Aqsa Flood is not automatically excluded from the defence. The statute does not establish that all independent research is automatically a reasonable excuse either.

The statutory language refers to the purpose of the activity, not possession of a university degree, university employment or academic accreditation. There is no express credential requirement in section 58(3A)(b)(ii). That does not mean every self-described research project necessarily qualifies as academic research. Its actual character and purpose would matter. This page has not identified a binding judicial definition that conclusively settles every borderline case involving independent researchers. The broader section 58(3) reasonable-excuse defence is therefore especially important for non-academic research. A longer treatment of section 58, including curiosity and the leading cases, is in The Anarchist Cookbook and section 58 of the Terrorism Act 2000.

entries.title: The burden of proof
entries.kind: Legislation · general explanation, not a finding about this defendant

paragraphs.text: Section 118 of the Terrorism Act 2000 creates an additional protection. If a defendant adduces evidence sufficient to raise a reasonable-excuse issue under section 58, the court or jury must assume that the defence is satisfied unless the prosecution proves beyond reasonable doubt that it is not. The defendant does not have to establish the excuse beyond reasonable doubt.
This is not a presumption that every researcher is acting lawfully. There must first be evidence sufficient to raise the defence.

entries.title: Particular publications: why wording can be legally ambiguous
entries.kind: Coverage limitation

paragraphs.text: While this case is active we do not publish, date, link or characterise particular posts, or offer a view on whether any post meets an element of any offence. That is the same choice explained in What we can say, and what we can’t. Withholding a publication does not mean it is relevant, admissible or among the charged counts.

A linguistic observation remains legitimate in general terms. An adjective of degree can describe an operation as extraordinary or unexpectedly successful, rather than morally admirable, and is not intrinsically an endorsement. A celebratory reading, including a conventional wish for someone’s success, could support an inference of approval or encouragement. Political context, such as characterising an operation as resistance, is relevant but does not itself establish a legal defence. Neither reading can be conclusively established from a caption alone. The defence could dispute the prosecution’s interpretation and argue that the required elements have not been proved.

Publicly reported particulars do not establish whether any particular publication forms part of the seven counts. The indictment and the prosecution’s particularisation of its case have not been obtained.

entries.title: Different offences, different rules
entries.kind: Legislation · general explanation, not a finding about this defendant

paragraphs.text: This is the central distinction for research of this kind. UK law does not impose a blanket prohibition on sending or reproducing anything originating from Hamas. Hamas is a proscribed organisation, but criminal liability for a particular publication or communication depends on the applicable offence and its elements.

For example, section 2 of the 2006 Act provides a specific defence in certain encouragement-based cases: where the person is not proved to have intended encouragement, and shows that the matter neither expressed their views nor had their endorsement, and that this was clear in all the circumstances. The defence applies only to the encouragement limb in section 2(3)(a), not to every category of terrorist publication. It is not a general exemption for research.
This is why a caption, contextual explanation or disclaimer may be relevant evidence, but cannot guarantee legality.

entries.title: Independent historical research: then and later
entries.kind: Our commentary

paragraphs.text: Suppose an independent researcher prepares a comparative historical study examining Hamas’s publicly stated objectives on 7 October 2023; what was known about the operation at the time; how Hamas, Israel, international media and independent investigators described the events; how these narratives changed by October 2025; and which claims were subsequently corroborated, contradicted or remain unresolved. That is a recognisable research purpose, even without an institutional affiliation.

The legal considerations change depending on the activity. Reading and archiving: section 58 may be relevant if material contains information of the statutorily specified kind. Research purpose and reasonable excuse matter. Analysing and describing: historical analysis and criticism are not automatically offences simply because Hamas appears in the subject matter. Publishing statements: sections 12, 1 and 2 become relevant depending on what is said, what is distributed and the required mental element. Redistributing original footage deserves particular caution. A video depicting an attack is not automatically a terrorist publication under section 2, but its content, accompanying commentary, intended effect and likely understanding by an audience may all matter.

For sensitive primary-source material, a written description, a carefully contextualised transcript excerpt or an independent analytical summary may achieve the research objective without unnecessarily redistributing the underlying footage.

entries.title: Should research have to be academic?
entries.kind: Our commentary

paragraphs.text: There is a genuine legal-policy tension. The statutory reference to academic research expressly protects a recognised activity. Yet public-interest investigations are frequently conducted by independent journalists, citizen researchers, historians, activists and people without institutional affiliations. A narrow approach could disadvantage independent researchers. An excessively broad approach, however, could allow almost any dissemination to be characterised retrospectively as research. The non-exhaustive wording of section 58 allows courts to consider genuine circumstances outside the expressly listed categories, without treating someone’s assertion that they are researching as conclusive.

Independent research can potentially attract a reasonable-excuse defence under section 58, without academic credentials. The same defence cannot be assumed to apply when publicly disseminating material or expressing views about a proscribed organisation.

For a publication on Independent Tribunal, the more precise legal question is: when does independent investigation of a terrorist organisation become criminal encouragement, support or dissemination, and what specific statutory protections exist for researchers outside academia? That is a more precise question than whether it is legal to research Hamas. It also keeps the analysis focused on the conduct, the statutory elements and the evidence, rather than the researcher’s identity.

Given the potential criminal consequences, any proposed publication incorporating original attack footage, or statements that could be interpreted as support, should be reviewed by a solicitor experienced in terrorism and media law. This is general explanation, not legal advice.

entries.title: A broad register with dated limits
entries.kind: Research method

paragraphs.text: The register includes Hamas-related proceedings, searches and arrests, Palestine Action expression and meeting cases, and related communications, performance and protest-condition cases. Grouped records explicitly identify co-defendants; distinct arrests of Peter Tatchell and investigations of Bobby Vylan remain separate. Counts describe entries in this collection, not UK defendants, prosecutions, offences or verified unique proceedings.

A source review on 10 November 2026 does not turn an older report into a current court-status certificate. Each machine-readable case record includes its jurisdiction, scope, legal provisions and the date of the last sourced position when known. Unknown dates stay unknown. Scheduled hearings are not proof that hearings happened.

The aim is comprehensive coverage of identifiable cases relevant to this subject. This edition is not an exhaustive national census. Further records need to be found through police and prosecution disclosures, court records and legal representatives; Scotland, England and Wales, Northern Ireland and Jersey require separate treatment.

sections.title: Tony Greenstein
sections.intro: A completed speech prosecution: read the allegation together with the acquittal.

entries.title: 21 August 2026 · not guilty
entries.kind: Reported jury verdict · Last sourced position: 2026-08-21 · England and Wales

paragraphs.text: Press Association reports that a Kingston Crown Court jury acquitted Tony Greenstein of inviting support for Hamas. The single count concerned three posts published on 7 October 2023 and material linked from them. The verdict followed two hours and eleven minutes of deliberation.

The report identifies Greenstein as a Jewish activist and the son of an Orthodox rabbi, aged 72 at trial. It records his contention that he did not support Hamas as an organisation, alongside the prosecution material, which included praise for the attack in a linked blog. The full exhibits matter when examining the dispute.

entries.title: What the acquittal leaves to investigate
entries.kind: Research method

paragraphs.text: Obtain the indictment, full posts and linked article as used at trial, prosecution consents, preparatory rulings, legal directions and formal verdict record. Examine the reasons for prosecuting and any documented costs or restrictions. The verdict alone does not explain which part of the prosecution case the jury rejected or establish bad faith by officials.

sections.title: What must the prosecution prove?
sections.intro: Start with the charged provision, the full expression and the circumstances in which it reached its audience.

entries.title: Inviting support and reckless encouragement are different offences
entries.kind: Legislation

paragraphs.text: Section 12(1) of the Terrorism Act 2000 concerns inviting support for a proscribed organisation, where the support is not confined to money or property. Section 12(1A) concerns expressing a supportive opinion or belief while reckless as to whether someone to whom it is directed will be encouraged to support a proscribed organisation. The provision also contains separate meeting offences.
Section 12 provides a maximum of fourteen years' imprisonment on conviction on indictment. This is the statutory ceiling, not a prediction of the sentence in any individual case.

entries.title: Images and footage are not automatic offences
entries.kind: Legislation and legal interpretation

paragraphs.text: An image of a flag, headband or uniform is not automatically unlawful: section 13 requires its particular reasonable-suspicion conditions. Nor does every sharing of footage or a statement establish encouragement or dissemination. Under sections 1 and 2 of the 2006 Act, the publication, circumstances, required intention or recklessness, and applicable defences must be examined. Section 1’s indirect-encouragement test includes whether glorified conduct could reasonably be understood as something to emulate.

entries.title: Section 13(1): the earlier Supreme Court ruling
entries.kind: Supreme Court judgment
entries.citation: Pwr; Akdogan and another v DPP [2022] UKSC 2

paragraphs.text: The Court held section 13(1) to impose strict liability, subject to knowledge that the person is wearing, carrying or displaying the article. It does not require the further mental element argued for by the appellants. The Court also rejected their Article 10 challenge. The reasonable-suspicion conditions still require proof; this ruling should not be collapsed into section 12(1A)’s recklessness test or assumed to resolve every section 13(1A) image-publication issue.

entries.title: Symbols, encouragement and dissemination have their own tests
entries.kind: Legislation

paragraphs.text: Section 13 addresses clothing, displayed articles and published images in circumstances arousing reasonable suspicion of membership or support. It is distinct from the section 12 invitation and reckless-expression offences. The wording and version applicable at the alleged event date must be checked.

Sections 1 and 2 of the Terrorism Act 2006 separately address encouragement of terrorism and dissemination of terrorist publications, with their specified intention or recklessness requirements. The content as a whole and the circumstances matter. An allegation under one provision should not be retold as a conviction under another.

entries.title: 26 February 2026 · the Supreme Court's explanation
entries.kind: Supreme Court judgment
entries.citation: R v ABJ; R v BDN [2026] UKSC 8

paragraphs.text: The Supreme Court dismissed the Article 10 challenges to section 12(1A). It explained that the expression must objectively support the organisation and that the defendant must know it does. The prosecution must also prove awareness of a risk of encouraging the intended audience and that taking that risk was objectively unreasonable in the circumstances known to the defendant.

Agreement with an organisation's aims, including Palestinian statehood or ending occupation, does not itself establish support for the organisation. Every ingredient must be proved to the criminal standard. Sentencing remains subject to proportionality. These appeals determined legal questions, not the defendants' guilt.

The published judgment contains a specific reporting-restriction notice concerning the underlying criminal proceedings. This section addresses the published legal ruling; further reporting requires checking the applicable orders.

entries.title: Northern Ireland: the police account and the disclosure gap
entries.kind: Official responses and limits of disclosure

paragraphs.text: A PSNI answer attached to a Policing Board question dated 6 November 2025 reported one Palestine Action-related arrest subsequently reported, fourteen ongoing investigations and an expectation of around twenty report files. Those are different stages and include a forecast. PSNI described evidence gathering and referral to PPS, with necessity and proportionality guiding decisions. This is its stated approach, not an independent finding that every intervention was proportionate.

PSNI’s March 2026 FOI/17010 response refused a combined request covering arrests, outcomes, costs, funding and guidance on cost grounds. It expressly suggested a refined request excluding the cost element. The refusal supplies no zero-case finding or usable arrest total. It gives a specific route for seeking the missing data.

In December 2025 PSNI had separately acknowledged holding section 13 guidance and described releasing redacted material while withholding information concerning investigations, policing tactics and personal data. The published FOI reply is cited here; its referenced guidance attachment has not been inspected. Redactions do not themselves establish improper enforcement.

sections.title: The case we are building
sections.intro: Our research question: did speech investigations and prosecutions impose unjustified restrictions on political expression, including where no conviction followed?

entries.title: Establish the words, the decision and the consequences
entries.kind: Research method

paragraphs.text: Collect the complete speech or post, its context and audience, the prosecution exhibit version, charge particulars, legal directions and outcome. Examine the strongest prosecution evidence alongside the defence response. An edited clip, an allegation and a jury verdict answer different questions.

Test the personal consequences through dated records: custody, bail conditions, seized devices, defence costs, lost work, study disruption and cancelled events. A claim that lawful discussion was deterred needs identified examples and evidence explaining why people changed what they said or published.

Trace complaints and official responses through documents. A complaint shows that action was requested; it does not, by itself, establish improper influence over an independent decision. Seek the reasons recorded by police, prosecutors and regulators, together with their responses to specific criticisms.

entries.title: An initial record, open to correction
entries.kind: Coverage limitation

paragraphs.text: This is an expanding collection of identifiable cases, not an exhaustive national register or a finding of misconduct. It contains named proceedings in England and Wales and Scotland, Northern Ireland referral data without a verified named case, and a separate Jersey comparator. Original case files and interviews remain to be collected. Additions require a source, jurisdiction, dated procedural position and a clear account of what remains unknown.
